vignette:
Marcus: A Consultant's Return

Marcus sits in the waiting room of his office tower each morning at 7:45 a.m., thirty minutes before his colleagues arrive. He tells himself it's about getting ahead on emails, but the truth is simpler: he needs the silence. At thirty-five, he's a successful tax consultant with a corner office on the forty-second floor, a position he'd worked toward for over a decade. His colleagues admire his precision, his ability to navigate complex regulatory frameworks, his reliability. What they don't see is how much effort it takes to sit in meetings without his leg bouncing, without scanning for exits, without that persistent hum of dread in his chest.

Three years ago, Marcus took a sabbatical. His wife Priya had been surprised but supportive when he announced he wanted to volunteer with an international relief organization in Syria. He'd felt restless in his structured life, hungry for meaning beyond spreadsheets and client calls. For eight months, he worked in a refugee camp, coordinating resources, documenting needs, translating for families who'd lost everything. The work was grueling and purposeful in a way his consulting practice had never been.

The attack came on a Tuesday morning in March. A mortar shell struck the clinic tent where Marcus was helping register patients. He remembers the sound-not loud, but wrong, a sound that didn't belong to the world. He remembers the smell of dust and something else, something burning. He remembers screaming, though he's never been certain if it was his voice. Three people died. A local nurse he'd worked alongside for months. Two patients. Marcus was thrown against a supply cabinet and walked away with lacerations and a concussion. The physical wounds healed quickly.

He returned to his consulting firm six months later, telling people he needed time to readjust. That was three years ago. The readjustment hasn't come.

Now, when Marcus sits in client meetings discussing tax implications for multinational corporations, his mind sometimes fractures. A colleague raises their voice in frustration about a deadline, and Marcus's body goes rigid. His hands grip the table edge. His vision narrows. He excuses himself, walks to the bathroom, and stands at the sink for ten minutes, running cold water over his wrists until he can remember where he is.

Priya has learned not to touch him when he's sleeping. The night terrors come three or four times a week-he wakes gasping, sometimes already halfway out of bed, convinced the tent is collapsing again. She's learned to let him wake naturally, to give him space. They haven't been intimate in fourteen months. He loves her, but his body doesn't trust anything anymore, not even her.

He avoids the news now, though he used to keep careful track of world events. He can't watch footage from conflict zones. He can't hear sirens without his chest tightening. He's become hypervigilant in ways he doesn't discuss-always aware of exits, of structural integrity, of how many people are in any given room. When a fire alarm test ran last month, he found himself in the stairwell, unable to stop shaking for hours.

Marcus is good at his job, still. His clients are satisfied. He makes excellent money. But there's a persistent exhaustion beneath everything now, a sense that he's living slightly outside his own life, watching himself perform competence while something deeper remains fragmented and afraid. He wonders sometimes if the person who came back from Syria is really him, or if Marcus the tax consultant is the one who died in that tent, and everything since has been a very convincing ghost.
